title: Climbing Stairs
statement: A staircase has n steps. Each move climbs either 1 step or 2 steps. Count the different sequences of moves that take you from the ground to the top step exactly. n is at least 1.

example.caption: With 4 steps there are 5 ways: 1111, 112, 121, 211 and 22. The table builds that count one step at a time.

output.label: dp[i] = ways to reach step i

idea.sentence: Let dp[i] be the number of ways to reach step i. Your last move came from step i - 1 or step i - 2, so dp[i] = dp[i - 1] + dp[i - 2].

jargon.plain: Solve small versions first, store each answer in a table, and build each new answer from stored ones.
What one table cell stands for. Here: the number of ways to reach step i.
The rule that says how a cell is computed from earlier cells.

watch.inputHint: One number: how many steps, e.g. 5

vars.meaning: number of steps in the staircase

compare.unit: calls (rough; the real brute force grows like 1.6^n, which 2n stands in for)

rows.name: Plain recursion
rows.note: Each call splits into two calls and the same step is solved again and again.

rows.name: DP table
rows.note: Each step is solved once, from the two cells before it.

rows.name: Two variables
rows.note: dp[i] only reads the two previous cells, so keep just those two numbers.

fast.takeaway: The two-variable form is where this ends up, but the table is the easiest way to see why it works.

stages.title: Base cells
stages.note: dp has n + 1 cells. The ground and step 1 each have exactly one way.

stages.title: Fill a cell
stages.note: dp[i] is dp[i - 1] plus dp[i - 2]: arrive by a 1-step or by a 2-step.

stages.title: Read the answer
stages.note: The last cell, dp[n], is the number of ways to reach the top.

edges.title: One step
edges.why: The table still needs two cells (index 0 and 1), so dp[1] must exist. That is why it has n + 1 cells.

edges.title: Two steps
edges.why: 1+1 and 2. This is the first cell the recurrence computes: dp[2] = 1 + 1.

edges.title: Counts grow like Fibonacci
edges.why: This already passes 2^30. It is fine in a 64-bit int, but a 32-bit int would overflow soon after.

edges.title: Table size
edges.why: dp = [1, 1, 2, 3]. Using n cells instead of n + 1 makes dp[n] fall off the end.

gotchas.text: Allocate n + 1 cells. The ground is index 0, so the top step n is index n. n cells means an off-by-one read.
new Array(n + 1) is full of holes. Use .fill(0) so every cell is a real number before you read it.
JS numbers are exact only up to 2^53 - 1. The count at n = 78 is already past that, so use BigInt if n can be that large.
make([]int, n+1) gives zeros, so you only set the base cells. int is 64-bit on 64-bit machines, but its size depends on the platform.

recap.pattern: 1-D DP: last move decides the cell
recap.key: dp[i] = ways to reach step i. It equals dp[i - 1] + dp[i - 2], because the last move was a 1-step or a 2-step.
recap.complexity: Time O(n). Space O(n), or O(1) with two variables.
moves: Cell meaning: dp[i] = ways to reach step i
Fill left to right: dp[i] = dp[i - 1] + dp[i - 2]
